title: Good Leaders Make the Implicit Explicit
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article argues that organizational culture rarely takes hold through posters or one-off value discussions -- it spreads only when leaders relentlessly translate abstract values into explicit, everyday behaviors. The author describes a practice of constantly narrating which actions reflect (or violate) stated values, and of pointing out exactly how deliverables do or don't meet quality standards. The underlying premise is that most of what shapes culture, including norms around meetings, conflict, and feedback, is left dangerously implicit in most organizations. The piece closes by urging leaders to test whether their own team could actually articulate the organization's unwritten rules.
points: Culture doesn't spread through posters or occasional speeches -- it spreads when leaders make values explicit in everyday moments.
Leaders should actively narrate which specific behaviors reflect (or breach) stated values as they happen.
Many of the norms that shape culture -- around meetings, conflict, feedback -- remain unspoken and untaught in most organizations.
A useful test: can team members actually articulate the organization's implicit standards and expectations?
quotes: From those values, good leaders are able to establish standards of quality, expectations for performance, and competencies that support personal and professional growth.
While a graphically designed list of the organization’s values that everyone can see looks impressive, it doesn’t do much to bring those values to life.
Good leaders go to great lengths to articulate the many qualities that define the organization’s culture and to make them explicit and transparent for everyone to see.
By constantly making the implicit explicit, the best leaders teach the culture rather than presuming it will manifest influence over time.
If culture is destiny for an organization, then making the implicit explicit is how that destiny best unfolds.
